newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Attack on rebel colonel's house rocks Tajik peace.
newsitem.headline: Attack on rebel colonel's house rocks Tajik peace.

text.p: A rebel colonel's house came under fire in Tajikistan on Thursday, jeopardising a fragile peace between his forces and government troops.

Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev blamed government forces for the automatic weapons attack in Kurgan Tyube, his stronghold 110 km (70 miles) south of the capital Dushanbe, just one day after a peace deal halted four days of fighting.
He accused the government troops, who are loyal to embattled President Imomali Rakhmonov, of failing to return to base under Wednesday's peace deal.

"They do not want to withdraw. I think the president is just powerless now. It is not his fault, it is the fault of certain commanders who want to take control of Kurgan Tyube," he told Reuters in Kurgan Tyube.
Asked what would happen if the government did not withdraw its troops, he said: "Honestly, I think it could only be war."

Fighting erupted between rival armed groups in Dushanbe on Saturday, just weeks after Rakhmonov signed a peace agreement with Islamic opposition guerrillas to end four years of civil war in the country of 5.7 million people bordering Afghanistan.

Khudoyberdyev, a 34-year-old commander who has mutinied twice before, was involved in fighting south of Dushanbe and later lost control of an aluminium smelter, one of few sources of revenue in the cash-strapped country.
The Tajik government said on Wednesday Khudoyberdyev had agreed to withdraw his forces to barracks after the peace talks and that he had accepted an order relieving him of his command.
But Khudoyberdyev told Reuters correspondents just before the attack on his house that he still considered himself in charge of the elite brigade he has commanded until now.
"As commander of the brigade, I say that I may even unite with the opposition and fight," he said.
After the interview, the Reuters correspondents heard Khudoyberdyev's forces fire an artillery gun in response to the attack on his house. There was no word of any casualties.
Khudoyberdyev said he wanted peace in Tajikistan but added: "If they do not withdraw tanks we will take measures."
Rakhmonov appears to have come through the fighting intact but peace remains hostage to Tajikistan's many armed groups.
Rakhmonov, 45, remains weak and dependent on several private armies which have subjected the mountainous country to gun law similar to that in Afghanistan.
The weekend fighting in Dushanbe, in which one rival warlord seized a northern district from another, was essentially a mafia-style battle for turf.
Russia has 20,000 troops in the republic, guarding frontiers and carrying out peacekeeping duties, but they stayed in the background during the fighting.
